key.situation: Your TV remote talks to the TV with a beam of light you can't see, at about 3.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
key.mission: Drag Frequency across the colours you can see, red to violet. Watch the energy per photon as the colour changes.
key.whatIf: you slide Frequency down to the remote's 3.2, below red and out of sight
key.impostorLine: Can't see it, so nothing's there.
key.trick: The real trick is knowing E = hf has no switch-off point: lower the frequency and each photon just carries less. Your eye can't use packets that small, but they're still there.

reveal.say: Drag Frequency down to 3.2. Watch the tag, the energy per photon and the wavelength.
reveal.expect: Tag reads Infrared • 3.2×10¹⁴ Hz, E = 1.3 eV per photon, Photon Energy 1.3 eV, Wavelength 938 nm.

key.situation: You tune engines at a workshop. Hotter exhaust means harder hits between gas molecules, and you want to know how much that buys you.
key.mission: Drag Average collision energy up from 0.3 and watch Success rate: where do the hits start turning into reactions?
key.whatIf: the hits could land ten times harder than the top of the slider allows

options.text: Too hard to stick, rate drops to 0%
Some still bounce off the wrong way

key.impostorLine: Enough energy, nothing can stop it.
key.trick: The real trick is knowing energy is only one gate; a hit also has to land the right way round, so wrong-way collisions fail however fast they are.

reveal.say: Drag Average collision energy to the top, 3.5× Ea, and let it run. Even here most hits bounce off.
reveal.expect: Success rate stays well under half at 3.5× Ea — most hits still fail, nowhere near 100%

key.situation: You read that in a 2019 trial, one two-week antibody course held off type 1 diabetes for about two years in people at high risk.
key.mission: Press Type 1 diabetes, lower Self-tolerance to 40% and watch which cells the T cells go after.
key.whatIf: the attack is in a nerve instead: Multiple sclerosis, with Self-tolerance right down at 0%

options.text: Every cell round the nerve gets hit
The nerve cell’s body is the target
Only the myelin coat is attacked

key.impostorLine: At 0% no self is safe. All of it goes.
key.trick: The real trick is knowing tolerance is lost to one self-antigen, so T cells hit only the cells carrying it: beta cells in the islet, myelin on a nerve.

reveal.say: Press No treatment, press Multiple sclerosis, take Self-tolerance to 0% and watch: the T cells go for the myelin and pass every other cell.

key.situation: Picture a house where one person is yawning by 8 pm and another is wide awake at 2 am, yet both get a full 8 hours.
key.mission: Press DSPS, then ASPD, and change Internal clock shift. Watch where the purple sleep window lands against the amber one.
key.whatIf: the pattern switches from DSPS to Shift work

options.text: The purple clock turns late, like DSPS

key.impostorLine: Every sleep problem is a bad clock.
key.trick: The real trick is knowing shift work is a healthy clock on the wrong roster: the purple body clock stays set to daylight and the amber required window moves.

reveal.say: Press None, DSPS, then Shift work. Watch purple settle at 23:00 while amber jumps to 08:00.
reveal.expect: SLEEP ONSET 23:00 · 9 H OFF THE 08:00 WINDOW

key.situation: You drop a ball. Its first bounce rises 1 m, and each bounce after rises r times the one before. You add up every rise, forever.
key.mission: Raise Common ratio r from 0.10 to 0.50 and watch Limiting sum S∞, the total of every rise.
key.whatIf: you swap in a bouncier ball with r = 0.90 — what do all the rises add up to

options.text: About 3 m, a little more than at 0.50
10 m, five times the total at 0.50
No total: the rises add up forever

key.impostorLine: Each step up in r only added a little.
key.trick: The real trick is knowing the total is 1 ÷ (1 − r): as r creeps up to 1 the gap 1 − r shrinks fast, so the total shoots up, yet still stops at one number.

reveal.say: Press Derivation and set Common ratio r to 0.90. Limiting sum S∞ reads 10.000: five times the 2.000 at 0.50.
